newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION-German pension reform update-by H. Jaeckel.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-German pension reform update-by H. Jaeckel.

text.p: By Hans Jaeckel, head of the domestic economic research group at DG Bank, Deutsche Genossenschaftsbank, Frankfurt

When Labour Minister Norbert Bluem's pension reform concept became known a few weeks ago, it looked as though it would be swept away by a flood of criticisms. Meanwhile, it has become clear that a large part of these attacks did not add up to give the concept the death blow, but rather neutralised each other.

What Bluem's proposal claims is that a contribution rate of about 22.9 percent and a pension level of 64 percent of net wage income are consistent and sustainable to keep the statutory pension system in balance. The fact that the concept was criticised both for lowering the level of pensions by too much as well as for not limiting the rise of contribution rates sufficiently proves that it managed to strike some sort of balance between those conflicting interests.

The remaining adversaries are not so easy to handle. Bluem's arithmetic presupposes that a larger part of the pension system's burdens will be taken over by the general budget, while Finance Minister Theo Waigel refuses to do so. With no extra funding from the side of general tax revenues, the figures would have to be changed - to a pension level of maybe 62 percent and contribution rates of, say, 23.5 percent. Waigel might also give in somewhat, and the problem becomes a matter of numerical compromise.

What remains are those critics who voice fundamental doubts about the viability ot the German pay-as-you-go pension system and ask for a (partial) shift to a funded system. Their line of argument has remained strangely vague in the current debate, making it possible for Bluem to dismiss the attacks as being just a philosopy but not a solution. But while Bluem is fiercely defending the current system, a large part of the population might find an alternative system quite attractive. To the normal citizen it seems obvious that pensions cannot be safe if the money that he holds a claim to in the future simply does not exist anywhere - as is the case in a pay-as-you-go system. Why not abolish mandatory contributions (disregarding the transition problem), and use the money thus saved to take individual precaution for old age?

On the macroeconomic level, matters are more complicated, however. The transition to a funded system would not change the basic economic fact that a population can only use the goods and services that are being produced - at home or abroad. Neither would it change the fact that the future is uncertain. Whoever buys fixed-interest securities to provide for old age cannot be sure about how many goods and services the money will buy him in the future. With variable-rate assets, there is additional uncertainty about their yields. Buying a house guarantees that one will have a place to live in the future. But should the necessity arise to sell the house and live in a nursing home, it is uncertain how much nursing services the value of the house will buy.

From this point of view, the difference between the two systems is really a "philosophical" one. In the statutory pay-as-you-go system, redistribution between the active and the retired generation is handled via legally enforced entitlements and obligations. In the private system, it works through individual contracts between borrowers and lenders. In the state system, balance has to be brought about by fine-tuning contribution rates and pension formulas. In the private system, balance is brought about by the equilibrating mechanisms of capital markets. In the state system, parliament decides. In the private system, individuals decide how much and in which form they want to make precautions for old age. In both cases there is no guaranteed standard of living for the future pensioner.

What is then left of the cause for a private, funded pension system? Firstly, the principle of subsidiarity. lf a growing part of the population is willing and able to take provision for old age into thelr own hands, the state should make it possible for them to do so. Secondly, the openness of a funded system to global capital markets which has the effect of de-coupling retirement incomes from adverse demographic changes within a single country. Thirdly, the expectation that in a funded system overall saving in the economy will be higher, overall capital formation will be promoted, enabling higher labour productivity and higher incomes in the future.

lt does not help the cause of the adherents of a private funded pension system to paint the picture of a system change during which the current active generation would be urged to finance the build-up of a huge additional capital stock, in addition to having to support the current retired generation. This scenario comes close to being a caricature of the basic idea and is too easily dismissed. The best that politicians or expert commissions could do today in order to open a perspective for the German pension system would be to acknowledge that the statutory pension system will have to be scaled down. Then, a few regulatory restrictions and tax conditions need to be changed to clear the way for a growing market for private old-age provision instruments. The generation that is entering the job market now should be in the clear that state pensions alone will suffice for a decent, but not for a good life after retirement.
(Dr. Hans Jaeckel is head of the domestic economic research group at DG BANK -Deutsche Genossenschaftsbank, Frankfurt. The views expressed here are those of the author alone.)
